item.title: Autumn Budget: Property industry demands action, not more uncertainty
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

As the UK property sector awaits the Chancellor's Autumn Budget announcement, industry leaders are calling for decisive action to stabilise the housing market. Estate agents, developers, landlords and mortgage experts have united in their plea for policy clarity, warning that continued uncertainty could further dampen market activity.

Property Taxation Under Review

Tax reforms top the agenda for many property professionals, with multiple organisations advocating for a comprehensive review of the current system. Propertymark has highlighted how successive changes to income tax, mortgage interest relief and stamp duty surcharges have created complexity for landlords and homeowners alike. The National Residential Landlords Association has joined these calls, while also pressing for Local Housing Allowance rates to better reflect today's rental market realities.

Industry bodies argue that piecemeal tax changes have contributed to a decline in private rental sector investment, potentially exacerbating the housing shortage. Many are urging the Treasury to consider the cumulative impact of property taxation rather than introducing further isolated measures that might have unintended consequences.

First-Time Buyer Schemes in Focus

The proposed Your First Home scheme remains a key talking point, though property professionals seek greater detail on how the initiative will operate in practice. While the prospect of 2.5% deposits for new-build properties could help first-time buyers, questions remain about:

  • Eligibility criteria for applicants
  • Regional price caps that reflect local market conditions
  • Long-term repayment obligations
  • Expected contributions from developers

Some industry figures have cautioned that stimulating demand without parallel measures to boost housing supply might simply push prices higher, potentially undermining the scheme's affordability objectives.

Mortgage Affordability Pressures

Mortgage costs continue to squeeze prospective buyers, with recent data showing significant increases in monthly repayments. For homeowners approaching the end of fixed-rate deals, the prospect of refinancing at higher rates presents additional financial challenges. Industry analysts suggest the Budget could address these concerns through measures that support both lenders and borrowers during this period of elevated interest rates.

As the property sector holds its collective breath ahead of today's announcement, the overarching message remains clear: the industry seeks stability, coherence and policies that consider the housing market's long-term health rather than short-term fixes. Whether the Chancellor's statement will deliver on these hopes remains to be seen.

item.title: Estate agency acquired by expanding property group after director’s 11-year ban
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Fylde Coast Homes Group has expanded its property portfolio with the acquisition of Stephen Tew Estate Agents, a well-established Blackpool-based agency. The deal sees the local business join the growing regional group whilst retaining its original branding and operational team. Founder Stephen Tew will remain as head of sales and operations following the takeover.

Business continuity amid expansion

The acquisition forms part of Fylde Coast Homes Group's strategy to grow through partnerships with established local agencies rather than starting new ventures from scratch. Directors Ged Mills and Steve Richardson emphasised that the Stephen Tew brand would continue operating under its current name, with customers dealing with familiar staff members.

In a joint statement, the directors explained: "This partnership allows us to maintain what already works successfully whilst providing additional investment and resources for future growth." The financial details of the transaction remain undisclosed, but the deal represents another step in the group's expansion across the Fylde Coast region.

Founder remains despite past disqualification

Stephen Tew continues his leadership role despite receiving an 11-year company director ban in 2021 relating to Covid Bounce Back loan investigations. At the time, Tew described the issue as an administrative mistake rather than intentional wrongdoing. The estate agency has traded under a new director since the disqualification, with Tew remaining as an agent within the business.

Tew commented: "Maintaining our brand identity, team and customer service approach was paramount in this agreement. Our clients will receive the same personal service they've always known, now supported by Fylde Coast Homes Group's resources." The founder confirmed he would retain day-to-day involvement in sales and operations.

Property professionals might view this acquisition as an example of how established local agencies can maintain autonomy whilst benefiting from larger groups' financial backing. The deal demonstrates how regional property networks continue to consolidate, often preserving respected local brands rather than absorbing them completely.

item.title: Property tax fears put housing market and investors on alert
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

As the chancellor prepares to deliver the Autumn Budget, industry experts are raising concerns about potential property tax changes that could unsettle the housing market. Estate agents and finance specialists warn that further measures targeting high-value homes, property investors or banks might dampen market activity during an already challenging period.

Prime property market faces tax pressures

The proposed High Value Council Tax Surcharge for English properties valued at £2m or more has drawn particular attention, with some fearing it may eventually encompass lower thresholds. Marc von Grundherr of Benham and Reeves cautioned that London's prime market, already bearing significant tax burdens, could see reduced investment appeal if additional measures target wealthy homeowners or overseas buyers.

"Rather than introducing further uncertainty, the government ought to foster confidence across all market segments," von Grundherr noted. These concerns emerge amidst ongoing market challenges, including elevated borrowing costs and broader economic hesitancy affecting buyer decisions.

Bank taxation could impact property finance

Financial sector taxation represents another area of potential concern for the property market. Jonathan Samuels of Octane Capital highlighted how increased banking taxes might inadvertently restrict lending capacity, affecting various market participants.

"From developers constructing new homes to investors refurbishing existing properties, the sector depends on accessible finance," Samuels explained. "Policies that raise financing costs or reduce lender appetite might ultimately hinder the housing growth the government aims to stimulate." The precise effects would depend on both the specific measures announced and how banking institutions choose to respond.

Inheritance tax concerns for rural landowners

Agricultural and rural landowners await clarity regarding potential inheritance tax adjustments, particularly concerning Agricultural Property Relief and Business Property Relief. Adam Morris of LandSale suggested that further modifications could complicate succession strategies for farming families and estate owners.

With multiple tax considerations potentially affecting different market segments simultaneously, industry professionals generally advocate for stability and measures that encourage rather than discourage housing market participation. As budget details emerge, homeowners and investors alike will be assessing how the announcements might influence their property decisions in the coming months.

item.title: Budget uncertainty leaves property buyers sitting on their hands
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

As the UK property market navigates economic headwinds, industry experts are calling for stability and confidence-building measures in the upcoming Budget. With higher mortgage costs and cautious buyers affecting transactions, estate agents suggest the chancellor should prioritise economic predictability over new housing initiatives.

Market Confidence Crucial for Recovery

Property professionals argue that restoring buyer confidence should be the government's primary focus. Adam Day of eXp UK highlights that both buyers and sellers require a stable economic environment to make informed decisions. "Further uncertainty around taxation or household finances could prolong the current hesitation in the market," he notes.

The sentiment is echoed across the sector, with experts observing that homeowners may wish to see clear, long-term policies rather than short-term interventions. With mortgage rates remaining higher than in recent years, predictable economic conditions could help potential movers assess affordability with greater certainty.

Changing Dynamics in Property Transactions

The current climate has led to noticeable shifts in how properties change hands. Auction House UK reports a 20% annual increase in auction stock as some sellers explore alternative routes to market. Oliver Prior, their managing director, notes: "We're seeing more post-auction negotiations as buyers reconsider their options in this environment."

Traditional sales are also undergoing changes, with Fine & Country's Nicky Stevenson observing that pricing strategies have become critical. "Competitively priced properties continue to attract interest, but the era of ambitious asking prices securing quick sales has passed," she explains. Buyers appear to be taking longer to commit, with many becoming increasingly selective about their purchases.

The rental sector isn't immune to these shifts either. Reports suggest smaller landlords are exiting the market while larger portfolio investors expand their holdings - a trend that could influence rental supply in coming months.

Calls for Regulatory Stability

Industry leaders are urging the government to avoid further regulatory disruption. JLL's Marcus Dixon emphasises that the housing market needs consistency after years of changes, particularly given current borrowing costs. Meanwhile, lettings specialists warn that financial pressures make client money protection more important than ever.

As the Budget approaches, the property sector appears united in its desire for measures that support stability rather than introduce fresh uncertainty. With affordability challenges persisting, many in the industry believe predictable policies could help rebuild market momentum in the months ahead.

item.title: BTL landlords call for tax overhaul as rental supply comes under pressure
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Property industry groups are urging the government to reconsider taxation policies affecting buy-to-let landlords, as dwindling rental supply creates intense competition among tenants. With the Autumn Statement approaching, calls are growing for a comprehensive review of how multiple tax changes have impacted the private rental sector.

Tax System Overhaul Needed to Boost Rental Supply

Industry bodies argue that successive tax changes – including mortgage interest relief restrictions and higher stamp duty on additional properties – have made long-term investment decisions increasingly challenging for landlords. Propertymark has called for a joined-up review of property taxation rather than piecemeal adjustments, examining how income tax, capital gains tax and stamp duty interact.

The National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA) reports that an average of ten prospective tenants now compete for each available rental property. NRLA chief executive Ben Beadle warned: "The tax system needs fundamental reform to encourage investment in new rental housing stock. With such intense competition for homes, the government must address supply issues if it wants to improve affordability for tenants."

The NRLA has also proposed unfreezing Local Housing Allowance rates, suggesting this could help over 900,000 households if payments reflected current market rents. Propertymark supports similar measures, recommending that housing benefit should cover at least the cheapest 30% of local rents, with annual adjustments.

Smaller Landlords Reassessing Their Positions

Industry experts warn that continued tax pressures may lead to further consolidation in the rental market. Sam Humphreys of Dwelly noted: "Smaller landlords with less efficient portfolios may reconsider their investments or exit the market entirely if taxation increases. While this could create acquisition opportunities for larger operators, policymakers should be cautious about measures that discourage overall investment in rental housing."

Roma Sharma of Rushbrook highlighted the growing financial pressures facing landlords: "Between rising maintenance costs, mortgage payments and taxation, the government must recognise that landlords provide an essential service – not just an additional revenue stream." Many in the sector argue that current policies risk reducing rental supply precisely when demand is at record levels.

As the government prepares its Autumn Statement, property professionals hope for a more strategic approach to housing policy – one that balances revenue needs with the importance of maintaining a healthy private rented sector. With rental shortages affecting tenants across the country, the debate around landlord taxation looks set to continue.

item.title: Understand Your Portfolio’s Cash Flow
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Expanding a property portfolio can be an exciting opportunity for investors, but it’s essential to approach it with a clear understanding of the risks involved. One of the most critical aspects to consider is cash flow management. Ensuring a steady income stream from your properties whilst maintaining financial stability can make all the difference in achieving long-term success. This article explores how homeowners and property investors can better understand and manage their portfolio’s cash flow.

Understanding Cash Flow vs. Returns

When managing a property portfolio, it’s crucial to distinguish between cash flow and overall returns. Cash flow refers to the immediate income generated from rental properties, minus expenses such as mortgage payments, maintenance costs, and letting agent fees. On the other hand, overall returns encompass both rental income and capital growth over time.

For many investors, focusing solely on capital appreciation can be tempting, especially in a rising property market. However, neglecting cash flow can lead to financial strain, particularly if unexpected costs arise or rental income fluctuates. A balanced approach that prioritises both cash flow and long-term returns can help build a more resilient portfolio.

Key Factors Affecting Cash Flow

Several factors can influence the cash flow of a property portfolio. Borrowers might consider the following:

  • Mortgage Costs: Interest rates and repayment terms play a significant role in determining monthly outgoings. Fixed-rate mortgages can provide stability, whilst variable rates may offer flexibility but come with the risk of rising costs.
  • Rental Income: Ensuring competitive rental rates is essential. Regular market reviews can help identify opportunities to increase income without risking void periods.
  • Property Maintenance: Unexpected repairs can quickly eat into profits. Setting aside a contingency fund for maintenance can help mitigate these costs.
  • Tax Implications: Changes in tax legislation, such as reductions in mortgage interest relief, can impact profitability. Staying informed and seeking professional advice can help optimise tax efficiency.

Strategies for Improving Cash Flow

For those looking to enhance their portfolio’s cash flow, several strategies could be worth exploring:

  • Refinancing: Reviewing existing mortgage deals and refinancing to secure lower interest rates or better terms could reduce monthly payments and improve cash flow.
  • Diversification: Investing in different types of properties or locations can spread risk and create more stable income streams.
  • Cost Management: Regularly reviewing expenses, such as insurance premiums and letting agent fees, can uncover opportunities to reduce overheads.
  • Energy Efficiency: Upgrading properties to improve energy efficiency can lower utility bills for tenants and make the property more attractive, potentially reducing void periods.

Managing cash flow effectively is a cornerstone of successful property investment. By understanding the key factors that influence income and expenses, and implementing strategies to optimise cash flow, investors can build a more sustainable and profitable portfolio. Regular reviews and professional advice can further support informed decision-making, helping to navigate the complexities of property investment with confidence.

item.title: Mortgage lenders are failing modern borrowers, shock findings reveal
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Mortgage lenders are struggling to keep pace with the evolving financial circumstances of modern borrowers, according to recent research. A study conducted by Nottingham Building Society reveals that 88% of mortgage brokers believe lenders are not adapting quickly enough to accommodate borrowers with non-traditional income sources. This lag in responsiveness could be preventing creditworthy individuals from accessing the housing market, particularly as self-employment and flexible work arrangements become increasingly common.

Brokers Highlight Growing Concerns

The research, which surveyed over 500 mortgage brokers and 2,000 UK adults, found that nearly seven in ten brokers (68%) anticipate borrowers with non-standard financial circumstances to become the norm. A significant proportion of brokers (31%) believe this shift has already occurred, while 49% expect it to happen within the next year. Despite this trend, many lenders appear unprepared to meet the needs of these borrowers.

Brokers identified several challenges when placing applications for clients with complex incomes. Initial affordability assessments were cited as the biggest obstacle by 19% of respondents, while the same proportion pointed to stringent evidence and documentation requirements. Additionally, 18% highlighted inconsistent documentation expectations between lenders as a key issue. These barriers suggest that even when brokers deem an application viable, borrowers may still face unnecessary hurdles.

Self-Employed Borrowers Hit Hardest

The consumer survey underscores the difficulties faced by self-employed individuals and those with irregular incomes. More than half (58%) of respondents believe lenders judge non-traditional earners more harshly than salaried employees, while 66% feel that variable or irregular earnings make securing a mortgage significantly more challenging. These perceptions are deterring many from pursuing homeownership altogether.

Over a quarter (27%) of respondents reported delaying, pausing, abandoning, or deciding against applying for a mortgage due to their income arrangements. Among self-employed individuals, this figure rises sharply to 49%. Furthermore, only 27% of adults believe the mortgage application process offers a level playing field, and just 25% feel lenders treat applicants with non-traditional incomes fairly.

Call for Greater Flexibility

With nine in ten brokers (90%) urging lenders to prioritise products that cater to a broader range of financial circumstances, the need for greater flexibility is clear. As the workforce continues to evolve, lenders may need to reassess their criteria to ensure they remain inclusive and accessible to all borrowers. Failure to do so risks alienating a growing segment of the population and exacerbating the challenges faced by those seeking to enter the property market.

The findings highlight the importance of adapting to modern income patterns to ensure that the mortgage process remains fair and equitable for all potential homeowners.

item.title: LSL Property Services buys back another 130,000 shares
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

LSL Property Services, a prominent player in the UK’s property and mortgage services sector, has recently expanded its share buyback initiative. The company acquired an additional 130,000 ordinary shares on the London Stock Exchange between 19th and 23rd October 2026. This move is part of a broader strategy announced earlier this year, reflecting the firm’s commitment to managing its capital structure effectively.

Details of the Latest Share Buyback

Through its broker, Shore Capital Stockbrokers, LSL purchased the shares at prices ranging from 253.6p to 258.7p per share. This represents a total investment of approximately £333,000. Unlike some buyback programmes where shares are cancelled, LSL has opted to hold these shares in treasury. This approach allows the company greater flexibility in managing its equity in the future.

Following these transactions, LSL now holds 7,303,897 ordinary shares in treasury. The company’s total issued share capital stands at 105,158,950, with 97,855,053 ordinary shares carrying voting rights. LSL has confirmed that any further shares purchased under the programme will also be held in treasury, maintaining consistency in its strategy.

What This Means for Stakeholders

Share buybacks often signal a company’s confidence in its financial health and future prospects. By reducing the number of shares in circulation, LSL may aim to enhance shareholder value. item.title: House price falls spread as growing supply puts sellers under pressure
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent data highlights a growing trend of house price declines across the UK, with over a third of homes now situated in areas where values are falling. This shift, driven by increased property supply and subdued buyer activity, is creating a more competitive market for sellers. According to Zoopla’s latest House Price Index, 35% of homes are located in postcode areas experiencing annual price drops—a significant rise from just 12% a year ago.

Buyers Gain the Upper Hand

The current market conditions are offering buyers greater flexibility and choice. Over the past four weeks, sales agreed have dropped by 7% compared to the same period last year, whilst the number of homes available for sale has increased by 7%. This imbalance is enabling buyers to negotiate more effectively, particularly as higher mortgage rates encourage them to be more selective. Estate agents are finding it increasingly challenging to advise sellers on appropriate asking prices, as overpriced properties struggle to attract interest.

Regional Variations in House Prices

While the national average house price remains 0.8% higher than a year ago at £273,100, this figure masks significant regional disparities. Southern England, particularly London and the South East, is bearing the brunt of the declines. In these areas, 85% of homes are located in postcode zones where prices are falling. London has seen a 1% drop in average prices over the past year, equating to a £5,400 reduction, whilst the South East and Eastern regions have experienced declines of 0.6% and 0.5%, respectively. Certain local markets, such as WC London, have faced even steeper falls, with prices dropping by 5.7%.

Conversely, more affordable regions are continuing to see price growth. The North West has recorded a 3.2% increase, adding £6,600 to average property values, whilst Northern Ireland leads the way with a robust 5.8% rise. Scotland has also experienced steady growth, with prices up 2.5% annually.

The Importance of Realistic Pricing

Despite the slower pace of sales, properties that are priced realistically are still finding buyers relatively quickly, with homes taking an average of 44 days to sell—on par with last year’s figures. Zoopla’s analysis underscores the importance of setting an appropriate initial asking price. Homes listed at least 5% below their estimated value between April and June 2026 were significantly more likely to secure a buyer within 90 days (41%) compared to those marketed at least 20% above their estimated value (26%). This suggests that sellers who adjust their expectations early in the process may stand a better chance of attracting interest.

As the market continues to evolve, homeowners may wish to carefully consider their pricing strategies in light of these trends. With buyers enjoying greater negotiating power and higher mortgage rates influencing decisions, setting a competitive asking price could prove crucial in achieving a successful sale.

item.title: Estate agency donates entire property sales fee to charity
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

In a notable act of community support, a north London estate agency has donated its entire commission from a recent property sale to a local charity dedicated to helping vulnerable young people. House Collective, the agency behind the gesture, chose to support Mary’s Charity, an organisation that works tirelessly with at-risk youth across north London. While the specifics of the property sale and commission amount remain undisclosed, the donation is set to bolster the charity’s efforts in tackling issues such as school exclusion, violence, and involvement with the criminal justice system.

Supporting Vulnerable Young People

Mary’s Charity provides vital support to young people facing significant challenges. In 2025 alone, the charity assisted 3,453 individuals, many of whom were at risk of school exclusion or violence. Notably, 95% of these young people came from low-income families. The charity’s initiatives include knife bins, which saw 231 weapons surrendered last year, and education programmes that helped over 200 young people achieve recognised qualifications.

Jason Allen, director of Mary’s Charity, emphasised the ongoing nature of their work. “Our mentors are available 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, and we remain committed to supporting young people, regardless of their circumstances,” he said. The charity has achieved a 64% success rate in reducing aggression among participants, with more than 650 young people completing accredited courses.

A Call for Greater Corporate Philanthropy

House Collective’s donation reflects its belief that businesses have a responsibility to give back to the communities they serve. The agency highlighted concerning trends in corporate charitable giving, citing research that shows FTSE 100 profits rose by 49% between 2014 and 2023, while charitable donations fell by 34% during the same period.

Jonathan Brandling-Harris, director at House Collective, explained the motivation behind the donation. “Primrose Hill has given us so much, and donating our full fee to Mary’s Charity is our way of giving back,” he said. “We can’t solve these issues alone, but we hope to inspire other businesses to contribute in their own way. If every business returned a portion of its success to the community it operates in, society as a whole would benefit.”

House Collective is now encouraging other businesses, including estate agencies, to support local charities through financial contributions, volunteering, or sharing professional expertise. The agency’s gesture serves as a reminder of the positive impact businesses can have when they prioritise social responsibility.

This story underscores the importance of community-focused initiatives and the role businesses can play in addressing societal challenges. As House Collective demonstrates, even small acts of generosity can make a meaningful difference in the lives of those in need.

item.title: Rightmove faces fresh questions over property listing figures
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Questions have emerged about the accuracy of property listing figures displayed on Rightmove, as rival portal MyPorta raises concerns over fluctuating numbers on the UK's largest property platform. The dispute centres on meta descriptions – snippets of text used by search engines – which allegedly showed significant variations in advertised inventory last year without clear explanation.

Discrepancies in property listing claims

According to MyPorta's analysis, Rightmove's website reportedly removed references to "over 900,000 properties for sale" and "200,000 to rent" from its meta descriptions in April 2025, only for these figures to reappear several weeks later. Archived webpage records suggest the numbers vanished from search descriptions between 23rd and 30th April, before returning by 20th May.

A separate claim regarding "over 900,000 new-build properties" was also identified on Rightmove's new homes page as recently as October 2025. These meta descriptions, while visible to search engines, don't necessarily reflect the actual number of live listings on the website at any given time.

Questions over portal transparency

Rightmove has stated the changes related to "a small number of historic meta descriptions" that have since been updated. However, MyPorta founder Mal McCallion has questioned the timing of these fluctuations, suggesting the figures' reappearance in May might have been related to website traffic patterns.

The debate touches on wider questions about how property portals present their inventory volumes and whether these figures could influence consumer behaviour. With Rightmove's average revenue per advertiser having grown substantially since 2010, some industry observers are asking whether listing claims play a role in maintaining the portal's market dominance.

While meta descriptions don't constitute formal claims about active listings, their visibility in search results means they could potentially affect how homebuyers and renters perceive a portal's market coverage. The Competition and Markets Authority has previously examined the property portal sector, though not specifically regarding listing disclosures.

For those comparing property platforms, it may be worth remembering that search engine descriptions provide limited insight into a website's actual content. Savvy property seekers might consider checking multiple portals and verifying listing availability directly with estate agents when searching for their next home.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The UK property and mortgage landscape continues to evolve, with recent developments highlighting notable appointments in both the prime housing market and affordable housing sector. These changes could have significant implications for buyers, sellers, and investors alike.

Experienced Agent Joins Savills’ St John’s Wood Team

Savills has announced the appointment of Simon Rosenblatt as a director in its St John’s Wood residential sales team. Rosenblatt brings over two decades of experience in the north west London property market, having spent nearly 20 years at Aston Chase. During his tenure, he specialised in high-value homes in NW8 and surrounding prime locations, overseeing several record-breaking transactions.

In his new role, Rosenblatt will collaborate with Stephen Lindsay, head of Savills’ St John’s Wood office, focusing on residential sales in St John’s Wood and Regent’s Park. His appointment strengthens Savills’ presence in prime London markets, which includes offices in Hampstead, Marylebone, and Primrose Hill. Rosenblatt expressed enthusiasm about joining Savills, citing its market position and team as unparalleled.

Pete Bevan, co-head of prime central London residential sales at Savills, highlighted Rosenblatt’s expertise and track record as invaluable assets for the firm. This move signals Savills’ commitment to enhancing its prime property sales operations in one of London’s most sought-after areas.

Stonewater Appoints New Chair Amid Affordable Housing Push

In the affordable housing sector, Stonewater has appointed Angus Michie as its new chair following a £350m funding award. Michie, who took up the role on 1 October, succeeds Sheila Collins after her seven-year tenure. The funding, secured through the Social and Affordable Homes Programme, will support the delivery of 2,348 affordable homes across Stonewater’s operating areas.

Michie brings a wealth of experience to the role, with 30 years in residential development. He currently serves as managing director of SevenCapital, a firm specialising in residential and mixed-use schemes across London, the Midlands, and the South East. Previously, Michie spent 25 years with Berkeley Group, gaining extensive knowledge of the UK housing market.

His familiarity with Stonewater, having served on its board and chaired several committees, positions him well to lead the organisation through its ambitious housing delivery plans. This appointment underscores Stonewater’s dedication to addressing the UK’s affordable housing shortage.

These appointments highlight the dynamic nature of the UK property market, with both prime and affordable housing sectors witnessing strategic leadership changes. Homeowners and buyers may wish to keep an eye on these developments, as they could influence market trends and opportunities in the coming months.

item.title: Dragons’ Den-style property investment show launches on Amazon Prime
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A new property investment series has made its debut on Amazon Prime Video, offering viewers an inside look at the world of property development and financing. Titled Property Elevator, the show adopts a format reminiscent of Dragons’ Den, where aspiring developers pitch their projects to a panel of seasoned investors. The programme spans five episodes, each showcasing entrepreneurs presenting their financial projections, costs, and potential returns in hopes of securing funding or entering into joint ventures.

The Panel of Investors

The panel features three prominent property investors, each bringing a wealth of experience to the table. Among them is Liv Cooke, a 27-year-old former freestyle football world champion who has successfully transitioned into property development. Cooke, the youngest investor on the show, founded Liv Cooke Properties, which focuses on residential projects, including accommodation for vulnerable individuals. While the show’s producers claim her property portfolio is valued at over £100 million, this figure remains unverified by independent sources.

Cooke is joined by Hayley Andrews and John Howard, both of whom have extensive backgrounds in residential and commercial development. Together, the panel scrutinises each proposal, assessing its financial viability, risks, and potential rewards. Cooke remarked, “Sitting on that panel, you see very quickly who really knows their numbers and who doesn’t. There were some deals that genuinely surprised me. I’m not afraid to say no, but when the fundamentals are right, I’ll back you all the way.”

The Format and Challenges

Property Elevator provides a platform for entrepreneurs to present their ideas whilst facing rigorous questioning from the panel. Each episode delves into the complexities of property development, from securing finance to managing costs and mitigating risks. The investors evaluate whether the proposed schemes offer sufficient returns to justify their backing, offering insights into the decision-making process behind property investments.

The show also highlights the challenges developers encounter when seeking funding, shedding light on the importance of thorough financial planning and realistic projections. By examining both successful and unsuccessful pitches, Property Elevator aims to educate viewers on the intricacies of property investment and development.

All five episodes of Property Elevator are now available to stream on Amazon Prime Video. For those interested in property investment or development, the series offers a unique opportunity to learn from experienced professionals and gain a deeper understanding of the industry.

item.title: Half a billion lost in stamp duty revenue since 2024 Budget
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK government has seen a significant drop in stamp duty revenue since the 2024 Budget, with estimates suggesting a loss of £541 million. According to Knight Frank, this decline is largely attributed to a fall in high-value property transactions following the Budget’s changes. This development raises questions about the broader impact on the housing market and government finances.

What’s Behind the Decline in Stamp Duty Revenue?

The drop in stamp duty receipts appears to be linked to a reduction in high-value property sales. Knight Frank’s analysis suggests that changes introduced in the 2024 Budget may have influenced buyer behaviour, particularly among those purchasing premium properties. Stamp duty, a tax levied on property purchases, is higher for more expensive homes, meaning a decline in these transactions has a disproportionate effect on overall revenue.

Whilst the exact reasons for the slowdown in high-end property sales are not entirely clear, experts speculate that increased tax burdens or economic uncertainty could be contributing factors. Additionally, changes to mortgage rates and lending criteria may have made it more challenging for buyers to secure financing for higher-value properties.

Potential Implications for the Property Market

The decline in stamp duty revenue could have wider implications for the UK property market. High-value transactions often play a key role in driving market activity, and a slowdown in this sector may ripple through other segments. For instance, sellers of premium properties might face longer waiting times, while buyers could find themselves with more negotiating power.

Furthermore, the loss of £541 million in tax revenue could impact government spending priorities. Stamp duty receipts are often used to fund public services and infrastructure projects, so a shortfall may require adjustments elsewhere in the budget. Homeowners and potential buyers might wish to monitor these developments closely, as they could influence future policy decisions affecting the housing market.

What Does This Mean for Homebuyers?

For those considering purchasing a property, the current trends in stamp duty revenue highlight the importance of staying informed about market conditions. Whilst the decline in high-value transactions may not directly affect buyers in lower price brackets, it could signal broader shifts in the property landscape. Borrowers might consider seeking professional advice to understand how these changes could impact their plans.

Additionally, prospective buyers may wish to explore their mortgage options carefully, especially if they are targeting higher-value homes. With lending criteria potentially evolving in response to market trends, securing favourable terms could become increasingly important.

The £541 million loss in stamp duty revenue underscores the dynamic nature of the UK property market. As high-value transactions decline, both buyers and sellers may need to adapt to changing conditions. Keeping an eye on future policy developments and market trends could help homeowners make informed decisions in the months ahead.

item.title: Rents rise 3.8% in 12 months to September
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Rents across the UK have seen a significant increase over the past year, with average monthly private rents reaching £1,406 as of September 2023. This marks a 3.8% rise compared to the same period last year, as ongoing challenges in the rental market continue to drive prices upwards.

Factors Contributing to Rising Rents

The surge in rental costs can be attributed to several key factors. A shortage of available rental properties has created a competitive market, pushing prices higher. Additionally, an increasing number of landlords exiting the market has further tightened supply. This combination of high demand and limited availability has left many tenants facing steeper rental bills.

Economic pressures, such as rising interest rates and inflation, have also played a role. Many landlords are passing on increased costs, such as mortgage repayments, to tenants, exacerbating the situation. This trend shows no signs of slowing, leaving renters to navigate a challenging landscape.

Implications for Tenants

For tenants, the rising cost of renting means a larger portion of their income is being allocated to housing expenses. This could lead to financial strain for some, particularly those on lower incomes or in areas where rental growth has been most pronounced.

Renters may wish to consider their options carefully, such as reviewing their budgets or exploring alternative housing arrangements. In some cases, tenants might find it beneficial to negotiate with landlords or seek longer-term tenancy agreements to secure more stable rental costs.

item.title: Prices falling in a third of postcode areas
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Recent data from Zoopla reveals that house prices are declining in 35% of UK postcode areas, with London and the South East experiencing the most significant drops. Meanwhile, northern regions continue to buck the trend, showing resilience and even growth in property values. This regional disparity highlights the uneven impact of current economic conditions on the housing market.

Regional Variations in House Prices

The latest figures indicate a clear north-south divide in the UK property market. London and the South East, traditionally strong performers, are now seeing prices fall in many areas. This shift could be attributed to higher property values in these regions, which may be more sensitive to economic pressures such as rising interest rates and cost-of-living challenges. In contrast, northern regions, including parts of the North West and Yorkshire, are experiencing price growth. These areas often offer more affordable housing, making them attractive to buyers seeking value for money.

Factors Influencing the Market

Several factors are contributing to the current trends in the housing market. The Bank of England’s recent interest rate hikes have increased mortgage costs, potentially deterring buyers in higher-priced areas. Additionally, the cost-of-living crisis may be prompting homeowners in the South to reconsider their budgets, leading to downward pressure on prices. Meanwhile, northern regions benefit from lower entry costs and strong local demand, which could be driving growth. Economic regeneration projects in cities like Manchester and Leeds may also be playing a role in boosting property values in these areas.

What This Means for Buyers and Sellers

For prospective buyers, the current market presents both opportunities and challenges. Those looking in northern regions may find more affordable options and potential for capital growth. However, buyers in the South may benefit from negotiating power in areas where prices are softening. Sellers, particularly in London and the South East, might need to adjust their expectations and pricing strategies to attract interest in a more competitive market. Working with a knowledgeable estate agent could help navigate these regional variations effectively.

As the UK housing market continues to evolve, staying informed about regional trends and economic factors is essential for making well-informed decisions. Whether buying or selling, understanding the local landscape can make a significant difference in achieving property goals.

item.title: Northern Ireland sales and rental markets thrive
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Northern Ireland's property market continues to show robust growth, with both house prices and rental rates experiencing significant increases. Recent figures indicate a 3.6% rise across the region, reflecting sustained buyer interest and the strongest tenant demand since records began in 2026.

House Prices on the Up

The Northern Irish housing market remains buoyant, with property values climbing steadily. Several factors contribute to this trend:

  • Competitive mortgage rates attracting first-time buyers
  • Relatively affordable prices compared to other UK regions
  • Strong local employment markets supporting purchasing power
  • Limited housing stock maintaining upward pressure on values

Prospective buyers might find it useful to monitor local price trends and consider speaking to a mortgage broker about the most competitive deals available. Those looking to purchase investment properties may wish to research areas with strong rental yields, as tenant demand continues to grow.

Northern Ireland's private rental sector has hit record levels of demand, with many letting agents reporting unprecedented interest from prospective tenants. The sector's growth appears driven by:

  • Young professionals preferring flexibility over homeownership
  • Students returning to campus-based learning post-pandemic
  • Workers relocating for employment opportunities
  • Families seeking temporary accommodation during house moves

Landlords might consider reviewing their property portfolios in light of these market conditions, though it's important to factor in recent regulatory changes affecting the private rental sector. Tenants facing rising costs could explore whether they're eligible for any local housing support schemes.

With both sales and rental markets performing strongly, Northern Ireland presents interesting opportunities for different types of property participants. As always, individuals are advised to conduct thorough research and seek professional financial advice before making any property-related decisions.

item.title: Agents urged to respond to government plans for new EV charging rules
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The government is seeking views on proposals that could significantly alter the rules around electric vehicle (EV) charger installations in rental and leasehold properties across England. Property professionals may wish to participate in the consultation before it closes on 16 December 2026, as the changes could introduce new obligations for landlords and managing agents.

Potential changes to EV charging rules

The joint consultation by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government and the Department for Transport considers both voluntary guidance and potential legislation. The proposals aim to streamline the process for tenants and leaseholders wishing to install EV chargers in properties with off-street parking. Key aspects under review include:

  • Statutory deadlines for landlords to respond to installation requests
  • Requirements to justify any refusals of permission
  • Clearer rules around allocated and demised parking spaces
  • Guidance for handling communal parking arrangements

While residents would typically cover installation costs, questions remain about ongoing responsibilities for maintenance, electricity supply and charger removal at the end of tenancies.

Impact on property professionals

Letting and managing agents might face increased administrative duties if these proposals become law. Potential new responsibilities could include processing applications, obtaining necessary consents and maintaining proper records of decisions. Particular challenges may arise in leasehold properties where installations require multiple approvals or upgrades to shared electrical infrastructure.

The consultation outlines possible grounds for refusal that landlords and agents might rely upon, including:

  • Insufficient electrical capacity in the property
  • Safety concerns about the proposed installation
  • Conflict with existing lease terms
  • Impact on limited parking provision

Propertymark, the professional body for property agents, is encouraging members to highlight practical challenges, particularly where proposed response deadlines may prove unrealistic in complex cases.

Marketing considerations for properties

These potential changes could influence how agents market properties with allocated parking spaces. It's worth noting that an allocated parking space doesn't automatically grant permission for EV charger installation – a distinction that may become increasingly important as demand for charging facilities grows.

Property professionals might consider reviewing their current processes and documentation to prepare for possible changes. With the consultation remaining open until December 2026, there's time for the industry to shape these proposals before any final decisions are made.

As the UK moves towards its net zero targets, these measures could play an important role in supporting the transition to electric vehicles while balancing the practical considerations of property management.

item.title: Hundreds of UK new-build homes linked to suspicious wealth
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

A recent investigation by Transparency International UK has revealed that hundreds of new-build properties across the UK are linked to suspicious wealth, raising serious concerns about money laundering checks in the property sector. The report highlights 708 homes and development sites valued at £2.2bn, spread across more than 150 locations and involving over 85 developers. These properties account for over a third of the 2,000-plus UK homes the organisation has connected to questionable wealth since 2016, with the broader portfolio exceeding £16bn in value.

Gaps in Anti-Money Laundering Checks

The findings suggest potential weaknesses in the current system for verifying the source of buyers’ funds, particularly when developers sell homes directly or market properties overseas. Transparency International UK has pointed out that many developers are not subject to the same anti-money laundering checks as estate agents, banks, and solicitors. According to their report, ‘Concerning Developments’, around three-quarters of developers are not registered with an anti-money laundering supervisor.

Off-plan sales, where properties are purchased before construction is complete, have been flagged as a particular risk. Buyers can acquire multiple homes across several transactions, and some may sell their interest before completion, meaning their names may never appear on HM Land Registry records. Additionally, developers relying on early sales to fund construction may face pressure to overlook potential red flags in order to secure deals.

High-Profile Cases in London

The investigation has brought to light several London developments where properties have been frozen due to links to sanctioned individuals or alleged criminal activity. For example, two executives associated with the Prince Group purchased 27 flats at Embassy Gardens in Battersea and Centre Point in central London. Following sanctions imposed by the UK and US over alleged human trafficking, fraud, and corruption, authorities have frozen all 27 properties.

Another case involves Elephant Park in south London, where 19 flats were bought through companies linked to an individual wanted in China on allegations of illegal gambling, which he denies. These properties have also been frozen by UK authorities. Such cases underscore the potential risks associated with overseas buyers and the need for stricter scrutiny of funds entering the UK property market.

Conveyancing Concerns

The report also raises questions about the role of conveyancing firms recommended by developers. Lawyers relying on developers for repeat business may face conflicting commercial pressures when verifying the legitimacy of buyers’ funds. This could compromise the thoroughness of due diligence checks, leaving the door open for illicit funds to enter the market.

As the UK property sector continues to attract significant investment, these findings highlight the importance of robust anti-money laundering measures. Homeowners, buyers, and industry professionals may wish to remain vigilant and seek independent advice to ensure transparency and compliance in property transactions.
